entries.title: White Sox hit 4 homers to beat Tigers, ensure 100-loss streak will end
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Whatever happens to the White Sox the rest of the way, their streak of seasons with 100 losses will end at three.</p><p>With their 9-5 victory against the Tigers, the Sox won their 63rd game of the season, ensuring they’ll finish with no more than 99 losses. If they continue to hit like they did Friday, they’ll finish well below that mark.</p><p>Asked whether snapping the skid was important, Miguel Vargas gave a fitting answer: “100%.”</p><p>“You guys know I’ve been here for [three] years, and I know how important this is for us,” said Vargas, who went 4-for-5 with two homers, a double and three RBI. “Not just for us, but for the entire organization.”</p><p>Munetaka Murakami hit his team-leading 27th homer, and Tristan Peters went 3-for-5 with his first homer since hitting for the cycle July 10. Braden Montgomery also went 3-for-5 with a triple and three RBI.</p><p>Manager Will Venable was happy to see the big game from Vargas, whose production since the All-Star break has paled in comparison to what made him an All-Star.</p><h3></h3><p>“We’re used to Vargy doing that every day,” Venable said. “And so for him to get back to who he is has been nice.”</p><p>The victory moved the Sox 3 ½ games ahead of the second-place Tigers.</p><h3>Urquidy earns win in debut</h3><p>The Sox called up righty Jose Urquidy from Triple-A Charlotte. Urquidy, whom the club acquired July 26 from the Pirates for righty Felix Doroteo, is best-known for his five seasons with the Astros (2019-23), for whom he pitched in the postseason each year.</p><p>Urquidy made his Sox debut in the victory against the Tigers, entering in the second inning after lefty Sean Newcomb started the bullpen game. He allowed three runs and five hits in 3 ⅔ innings, earning the win because he was on the mound when the Sox scored five runs in the fourth to take the lead.</p><p>“Urquidy is going to throw strikes,” Venable said. “And with that comes some hits, too. I thought he did a really good job just continuing to compete in the zone. Probably had more in the tank, but he did his job.”</p><h3>Blister puts Martin on IL</h3><p>Not everyone believes it, but the blister on right-hander Davis Martin’s middle finger was bad enough for the White Sox to put him on the 15-day injured list Friday.</p><p>Martin said he noticed the blister in the second inning of the Sox' 9-8 loss to the Reds on Thursday. He blamed it and poor command for beaning the Reds' Sal Stewart, which got him ejected in the third inning.</p><p>“There’s a good chunk of skin gone,” Martin said. “A lot of questions popped up where it just made sense to put me on the IL and get it taken care of.”</p><p>The Sox continued to plead their case that Martin did not intend to throw at Stewart, even though, in the umpires’ estimation, he admired his homer in his first at-bat a little too long.</p><h3>More roster moves</h3><p>The Sox made four other roster moves, sending rookie righty Tanner McDougal back to Charlotte, calling up lefty Tyler Schweitzer, claiming former Red Sox catcher Jake Rogers off waivers and designating lefty Joe Rock for assignment.</p><p>After trading for Joey Bart at the deadline, only to watch him get hit by a pitch that broke his left hand, the Sox will give Rogers a try as they wait for Kyle Teel to return from a sprained left ankle.</p><p>“Really good defensive catcher,” Venable said of Rogers, who also has played for the Tigers and Orioles this season. “You look at our catching unit, and to be able to add depth is really important for us.”</p><p>Rogers is expected to arrive Saturday. He’ll force another roster move, between Edgar Quero and Drew Romo. entries.title: Dialysis patient found bound, gagged in south suburbs after robbery in Chicago, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was allegedly taken and later found bound and gagged outside a Harvey home on Friday after being robbed in Chicago, police in the far south suburb said.</p><p>Harvey police responded to a call in the 15500 block of Loomis Ave. at 4 p.m. and found a man on the porch of a residence, police said in a news release.</p><p>The unidentified man, estimated to be in his late 30s to early 40s, was taken to Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn for treatment. The man was described by police as a dialysis patient. The extent of any injuries he might have sustained was unclear.</p><p>Officers said the man was in robbed in Chicago, then restrained and transported to the porch in Harvey.</p><p>“This was a deeply disturbing incident,” Harvey Police Chief Dale Mitchell said the news release. “Our officers responded immediately, secured the scene and ensured the victim received medical attention. Our investigation has determined that the underlying incident occurred in Chicago, and we will be coordinating with the Chicago Police Department as the investigation moves forward.”</p><p>The incident appeared to be isolated, and investigators are trying to determine a motive, police said. </p><p>No descriptions of possible suspects was provided.<br></p>

entries.title: 10-year term limit for House speaker, Senate president more than sufficient
entries.summary: <p>After Michael J. Madigan’s 36 years as Illinois House Speaker, a 10-year term limit on current and future speakers doesn’t seem like a lot of time in the big chair.</p><p>Except it is.</p><p>Nobody prior to Madigan had ever served 10 years as speaker in this state, going back to when Illinois became a state in 1818. The only person who came close was Republican Warren Wood, who held the position for eight years in the 1950s.</p><p>Most of the rest served single terms or two terms. Democrat Paul Powell, served six years, including two years before Wood and four years after. Powell became infamous for stashing cash in shoeboxes at his Springfield hotel residence and died with an estimated fortune of $4.6 million. But I digress.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-df0000" name="module-df0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Another Democrat, Bill Redmond, also held the gavel for six years, although Madigan held quite a bit of sway over him in the late 1970s. Two Republicans served as speaker for six years each in the early 1900s.</p><p>But that’s about it. Republican George Ryan was speaker for two years before he was tapped to be Gov. Jim Thompson’s running mate. In the 1930s, four different members (three Democrats and one Republican) held the gavel for just two years each. Out of 70 House speakers, 47 served two years or less (four days in the case of Ryan’s Majority Leader Art Telcser).</p><p>What I’m getting at is 10 years is actually a long time.</p><p>More importantly, though, the 10-year ceiling has also somehow become a floor — an expected decadelong entitlement.</p><p>House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch has obviously fully intended to serve the full decade since he was first elected to the chamber’s top job for a two-year term in 2021. You may have noticed that a couple of his members who spoke out early about his mishandling of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" >Harry Benton</a> sexual harassment matter suddenly went silent. That was no coincidence. Pressure is being exerted on the rank-and-file. His team wants those 10 years.</p><p>But a decade with the gavel is not only historically unique, it’s also longer than the average service time for House Democratic members, currently 8.4 years. That’s up a bit from a six-year average in 2020, according to the statehouse’s unofficial honorary historian (a title I just made up) John Amdor. But it’s still below the 10-year House speaker term limit.</p><p>Starting in the final two decades of the previous century, the Senate has a history of electing Senate presidents to multiple terms. Democrat Phil Rock held the Senate’s gavel for 14 years. Then, Republican Pate Philip served 10 years before the Democrats won the right to draw the new district map in 2001. Democrat Emil Jones was the chamber’s top person for six years, and was replaced by Democrat John Cullerton for 11 years. Current Senate President Don Harmon was first elevated in 2020, but he’s eligible to serve until 2031 because that first year after Cullerton resigned midterm doesn’t count toward the chamber’s 10-year term limit.</p><p>Before Rock, most Senate presidents served just two to six years, except for the 10 years that Republican Sen. Art Bidwell held the gavel from 1955-1965.</p><p>One of the reasons that House speakers and Senate presidents served such short stints was that party dominance wasn’t assured like it has been for the last several decades. Partisan majorities flipped back and forth much more before the advent of computer-driven redistricting. Republicans and downstate Democrats would also occasionally scheme to prevent Chicago from holding power in their chambers (which is how Powell was first elected speaker).</p><p>I’m not advocating here for reducing the term limits to six years or whatever. But what I am saying is that Illinois government will not crash and burn if Welch and Harmon don’t serve their full five two-year General Assemblies as their chambers’ leaders.</p><p>They should both have to earn each and every one of their two-year terms. A 10-year stint should not be considered the minimum length of service. If their members want both of them to stick around, that’s their decision, as long as they recognize that nobody is automatically entitled to a decade at the top.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-760000" name="module-760000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: White Sox need Colson Montgomery to find his timing before it's too late
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Colson Montgomery hadn’t hit sixth in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> lineup since April 22. But that’s where he has found himself in four of the last five games, including the opener of a big three-game series Friday against the second-place Tigers.</p><p>“I talked to Colson the other day and just said, We’re going to move you down a spot or two in the order,” manager Will Venable said Thursday. “No big deal. Just want to take a little pressure off him not to feel like he had to do anything more than just get back on line and be himself.”</p><p>It hasn’t quite worked. After hitting a three-run homer batting sixth Sunday, Montgomery is hitless in his last 15 at-bats in that spot. In 115 games overall, his batting average is down to .209, and despite hitting 26 home runs, his slugging percentage is down to .431.</p><p>In five at-bats Friday, he struck out twice, flew out twice and grounded out.</p><p>In 71 games last season, his rookie year, Montgomery batted only .239, but he slugged .529 and hit 21 homers. This season, he’s striking out more, he’s walking less and he isn’t hitting the ball as hard.</p><p>Call it a sophomore slump if you want, but judging by Montgomery’s frustrated reactions after many at-bats, it looks like more than that. And for the Sox to maintain their hold on first place in the American League Central, they need him to figure it out soon. Time is of the essence.</p><p>“Colson knows he’s not performing to the level he is capable of performing,” Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon told the Sun-Times. “Your sophomore season, you expect some form of regression as the league starts to learn more about you. But right now is really just a timing thing for him — the timing of his move and getting to a spot where you can fire when you want to fire. For some guys, it’s when they initiate their move relative to the pitcher.”</p><p>Montgomery has said those frustrated reactions aren’t because of the result of the at-bat, but because he didn’t follow his process. But truth be told, both have become problems.</p><p>“You have the mechanical side of things, and then you have the approach side of things,” Shomon said. “Timing goes inside of that. I think he gets frustrated when he gets away from his plan and he starts maybe trying to do too much. What causes him to do too much is overthinking inside the at-bat. He knows that when those things are in place, he’s going to put together a good at-bat.”</p><p>Since the 2025 All-Star break, Montgomery ranks fifth in the majors with 47 home runs. A run of homers would be a pretty good sign that his timing is back. But what would indicate that without a 400-foot blast as evidence?</p><p>“Good swing decisions and stung balls the other way,” Shomon said. “More like left field, center field. We saw it earlier — that walk-off against the Angels. He got a breaking ball, line drive up the middle. Those little moments. That’s when you know Colson is in a good spot.”</p><p>The thing is, that happened April 29. We’re a long way from that.</p><p>Venable hasn’t hit Montgomery lower than sixth this season, and given his devotion to handedness — Venable tries to avoid pockets of hitters on the same side of the plate — he probably won’t.</p><p>By the sound of it, Montgomery won’t hit — or not hit — his way out of the lineup, either.</p><p>“We still have all the faith and trust in Colson,” Shomon said. “He’s a young hitter playing at the highest level in baseball. There’s no doubt Colson’s going to continue to work through it, and he’s going to get out of it. No one’s free of this. Guys go through this stuff.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Chicago startup's NHL deal creates new way to bet on sports teams' performance
entries.summary: <p>Hockey fans and everyday investors could soon trade on the performance of the Blackhawks or other NHL teams through futures contracts.</p><p>Chicago-based startup FutureSports announced a landmark deal last week with the NHL that would use official game statistics to establish financial indexes on the league's 32 teams — a first in finance and sports. It comes on the heels of FutureSports' partnership with Loop-based CME Group to offer sports futures contracts. CME operates the world’s largest futures exchange.</p><p>Futures contracts, tied to the value of indexes, allow investors to buy or sell an asset at an agreed price by a specific date. It also allows traders to hedge risks.</p><p>For decades, futures contracts have primarily been associated with agriculture products, like corn and soybeans, or energy commodities, such as oil and natural gas, as well as stock indexes like the S&P 500. Futures even got the Hollywood treatment with the 1983 film "Trading Places," when Dan Aykroyd and Eddie Murphy's characters cashed in on orange juice futures, and over 20 years later, inspired a federal provision nicknamed the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-MB-18853" target="_blank" >Eddie Murphy Rule</a>.</p><p>FutureSports and CME's new offering means if the Blackhawks play poorly, for example, a season ticket holder could take a short position on the team's index to try and recoup some of their ticket investment losses. Corporate sponsors, which spend millions annually on sports deals, could buy hockey futures to limit their exposure if a key athlete gets injured or the team just fails to meet expectations. </p><p>The companies highlighted other potential market participants like garage and parking lot operators, retailers and even the sports franchises.</p><p>"We believe we've hit a chord with sports as the underlying asset class or sports performance,” FutureSports co-founder Rhett Dinsdale said. “It gives people and the financial community access to that sports statistical performance that's never existed before.”</p><p>CME plans to list the futures, pending regulatory review, on Sept. 28 — a day before the puck drops in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nhl" target="_blank" >NHL</a> season opener.</p><h3>How it works</h3><p>The indexes will open at 7,500 points and fluctuate throughout a game, based on real-time statistical data. FutureSports plans to share every stat category and their correlation on the index, before trading starts next month. </p><p>“It all comes down to education,” FutureSports co-founder Leigh Taylforth said. “It will be a slow and deliberate approach."</p><p>Unlike contracts on prediction markets, futures focus on asset price changes and require margin, or collateral, of several thousand dollars. Prediction market contracts are yes-or-no wagers on whether a real world event will happen and typically trade between $0.01 and $1.00.</p><p>CME said the sports futures will be available in standard-sized contracts at 10 times the value of the underlying NHL indexes, while microsized contracts geared for retail traders will be 1/10 the value of those indexes. And participants can trade around the clock.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-100000" name="image-100000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6dae3dd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4aa5fe2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01b8d93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of CME Group headquarters at 20 S. Wacker Drive in the West Loop." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01b8d93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4b579d0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/01b8d93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+712/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2Fed%2F0962a6eb400aa395a82d69c494b1%2Ffsindex-260815-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>CME Group is headquartered at 20 S. Wacker Drive in the West Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>NHL spokesperson Jen Neziol said players, coaches and staff will be prohibited from buying or selling sports futures.</p><p>The league will only provide FutureSports underlying statistics and isn't involved in the “determination, calculation or governance of the indexes,” according to a news release. It'll also establish “layered monitoring and other protections” to support the integrity of games and related financial products.</p><p>The Blackhawks didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Trading futures is complex and its investors are savvy. Even retail traders, who buy for themselves and often make smaller trades, use similar financial analysis tools as institutional investors. </p><p>“Anyone considering trading them should understand the mechanics, costs and risks first and seek professional guidance as appropriate,” said Joseph Cusick, senior vice president and portfolio specialist at Calamos Investments in Naperville. “Futures traders can experience rapid gains or losses because of margin requirements.”</p><p>The margin is typically 3% to 10% of the total contract value. Institutional investors will be required to front thousands of dollars for their sports futures trades, while the margin for microsized contracts will be much smaller.</p><p>FutureSports said it also plans to create indexes tied to select NHL athletes, with CME rolling out associated contracts based on those indexes. It's also targeting partnerships with other leagues, though an index for the Bears and other NFL teams won't happen this season, Taylforth said. </p><p>Matthew Rice, chief investment officer at Goldstone Financial Group in Oakbrook Terrace, expects sports futures to draw customers from retail trading platforms like Robinhood but winning over institutional investors, which comprise 94% of CME’s trading volume, is another challenge.</p><p>“There has to be some sort of structural reason, like a positive embedded rate of return, to come out of it before we can expect it to become more institutionalized,” he said.</p><h3>‘Started from scratch’</h3><p>FutureSports started in 2022 by Dinsdale and Taylforth, who were living in Australia. They traveled to Chicago regularly to meet their legal team and became enamored with the city’s welcoming vibe, professional talent and sports culture — key factors that led them to relocate the business here in 2023.</p><p>“We’ve always been familiar with Chicago as the home of derivatives globally,” Dinsdale said. “The access to talent here is second to none. And Chicago is a great sports town.”</p><p>Both have extensive career experience in derivatives trading for market makers, investment banks and hedge funds.</p><p>“We actually came out here with no contacts within the sports industry,” Taylforth said. “So we started from scratch in sports.”</p><p>The duo relied on introductions and found an immediate reception pitching sports leagues and eventually investors, like Red Sox owner John Henry, a pioneer commodities futures trader for over 30 years.</p><p>”John Henry was probably the easiest pitch,” Dinsdale said. “He revolutionized commodities markets from quant trading.”</p><p>Their pitch has also attracted financial backers such as Cubs ownership's Marquee Ventures, Elysian Park Ventures, the investment arm of the Dodgers ownership group, platforms like Robinhood and financial firms, including CME.</p><h3>Good odds</h3><p>It's not the first time a Chicago company has proposed sports futures.</p><p>In 2020, Eris Exchange pitched sports futures that essentially mimicked sportsbook bets, contending casino operators and other parties economically impacted by NFL games should be allowed to hedge their positions. </p><p>But the Commodities Futures Trading Commission voiced concerns that the trades amounted to sports gambling, prompting Eris to withdraw its proposal. The five-member commission, a sister agency to the Securities and Exchange Commission, regulates the derivatives and prediction markets.</p><p>Cboe acquired Eris, later rebranded Cboe Digital, in 2022 but leveraged the takeover to launch new digital asset products, including listing and clearing a suite of bitcoin and ethereum futures.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div >NinjaTrader</a>, exclusively serving retail futures traders, said more than 36% of its customers are under 35. A year ago that demographic accounted for 28.4%, CEO Marty Franchi said. The Loop-based company counts nearly 4 million annual users.</p><p>The percentage of its traders aged 18 to 24 have doubled in the last few years.</p><p>“We’re seeing the age of the consumer get younger, as there’s more access and innovation in favor of retail,” Franchi said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-550000" name="module-550000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>Futures exchange: Understanding what it is and how it works</h4><br><b>What is a futures exchange?</b><br><br>A futures exchange is a marketplace where traders can buy and sell contracts of an asset at a predetermined price on a future date. It allows participants to manage risks such as price swings associated with financial or agricultural products. And some trade futures to speculate on price movements.<br><br>All types of commodities can be traded in futures contracts like wheat, soybeans or energy sources, such as natural gas and crude oil.<br><br>Futures markets also cover precious metals, financial securities like treasury bonds and stock indexes, as well as currencies.<br><br>“No one is necessarily planning to take delivery of barrels of oil or truckloads of corn,” Phil Battin, CEO of Ambassador Wealth Management in Warrenville, said. “Many participants simply use futures to manage financial risk or express an opinion about where prices are headed.”<br><br>Commodities are listed on indexes, composed of numeric values that represent a group of assets and measure their performance over time.<br><br>“Because you cannot physically own an index, index futures and options are generally settled financially rather than through delivery of an asset,” said Matt Herman, senior advisor and certified public accountant at the Loop office of Moneta, a wealth management and financial services firm.<br><br>The S&P 500 index, which tracks the stock performance of 500 leading companies listed on U.S. exchanges, is perhaps the most well known.<br><br>Dan Passarelli, CEO of Market Taker Mentoring in Frankfort and a former floor trader at Cboe Global Markets, said an index serves as the “underlying value” for derivatives products, such as futures and options.<br><br>“In simple terms, that value changes as the stocks in that basket of 500 stocks change value,” he said.<br><br><b>How does it work?</b><br><br>Only members of an exchange, like brokers and commercial traders, are allowed access. And they need to be registered with National Futures Association and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. <br><br>The size of a futures contract is standardized but would vary depending on the commodity and exchange.<br><br>Institutional trades typically have contract values of $100,000 to over $250,000, though the actual amount of money paid to enter a trade is much smaller, typically 3% to 10% of the total value. It’s common for institutional traders — private equity firms, hedge funds and pension managers — to implement risk management strategies by deploying hundreds or thousands of concurrent trades.<br><br>Retail investors, who use their own money, generally access markets through a futures commission merchant or brokerage firm, which typically assess their experience, financial resources and risk awareness before approval.<br><br>Retail contracts are much smaller, 1/10 to 1/100 the size of standard futures contracts. Their growth has proliferated in the last decade as exchange operators like CME Group and Cboe launched micro- and mini-contracts that are more accessible and less costly to execute.<br><br>Both contracts have margin, or collateral, requirements, and while it’s less burdensome for retail traders, they would still have to put in thousands of dollars to cover the margin.<br><br>An initial margin amount of $3,700 could allow an investor to purchase a futures contract for 1,000 barrels of oil valued at $45,000, with oil priced at $45 a barrel. If oil prices are trading at $60 when the contract expires months later, the trader has a $15 gain or $15,000 profit, according to an Investopedia example. But if oil prices fall, the trader is on the hook for the difference. <br><br>“The more important question is not whether someone can trade them, but whether they understand them well enough to do so,” Herman cautioned. “These instruments can be useful for hedging and managing risk, but leverage can also magnify losses quickly.”</div> </div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/03/wrigleyville-bar-rizzos-fans-mexico-england-world-cup-match-kalshi" >Wrigleyville bar plans to give fans $100 if Mexico wins World Cup match, with help from Kalshi</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/01/28/white-sox-cme-group-sign-multiyear-sponsorship-deal-for-teams-first-jersey-patch" >White Sox, CME Group sign multiyear sponsorship deal for team’s first jersey patch</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/technology/2024/06/26/cme-group-google-join-forces-data-center-expansion-aurora-cloud-computing" >CME Group and Google join forces on data center expansion in Aurora</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Districtwide CPS support needed for the arts — not just at one high school
entries.summary: <p>On July 31, the Chicago Board of Education proposed providing $5.5 million to sustain Chicago Arts High School — formerly ChiArts — for one year under its current model. More than half of the Department of Arts Education budget would be redirected to support one school, limiting investments that expand arts education across the district. The board <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/07/30/chiarts-funding-vote-postponed-as-cps-board-debates-budget-consequences" >postponed a vote until Aug. 27</a>.</p><p>No one wants to see students lose access to a school that provides meaningful opportunities for young artists. When the high school’s board voted not to renew its operating agreement with Chicago Public Schools, the district rightly stepped in to ensure students could continue their education.</p><p>But should solving one school’s financial challenges come at the expense of arts opportunities for students across Chicago?</p><p>Just over a year ago, the CPS board unanimously adopted a five-year <a class="Link" href="http://arts.cps.edu/" target="_blank" ><u>Arts Education Plan</u></a> committing to equitable access to high quality arts education in every neighborhood. That commitment has produced measurable progress. At <a class="Link" href="https://www.ingenuity-inc.org/data-research/state-of-the-arts-reports/2024-25/" target="_blank" ><u>Ingenuity</u></a> — our nonprofit that pushes equity in public school arts education — data shows a 23 percentage point increase in arts staffing at CPS schools over the past six years. Yet the work is not complete: Only 39% of schools have reached the highest level of arts education.</p><p>Chicago Arts High School serves about 520 students. The Department of Arts Education supports a districtwide strategy serving more than 316,000 students.</p><p>Redirecting districtwide funding may close this year’s gap, but it does not resolve the underlying structural challenge. History also shows that budget shifts are rarely temporary; once funding is redirected, it can be extraordinarily difficult to restore those dollars to districtwide initiatives.</p><p>This is not a debate about whether CPS values the arts. It does. It is not a debate about whether Chicago Arts High School provides meaningful opportunities for students. It does. The question is whether Chicago will allow one school’s financial challenges to diminish opportunities for students across the district.</p><p>CPS must protect its commitment to arts education for every student while ensuring that every school operates sustainably, equitably and in alignment with CPS' public mission.</p><p><i>Nicole Upton, executive director, Ingenuity</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d40000" name="module-d40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Strong financial ecosystems spur housing </h3><p>WBEZ's Alden Loury's recent column headlined, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/08/housing-south-west-sides-chicago-black-communities-alden-loury" >“Without housing on South, West sides, Chicago’s Black communities won’t grow”</a> accurately highlights the stark population and housing loss across the South and West sides. But focusing primarily on residential construction puts the cart before the horse.</p><p>Building homes alone will not reverse population decline if the underlying economic conditions such as access to business capital, commercial corridors, public safety and employment anchors remain unaddressed. People move where economic opportunity, service access and wealth creation exist. </p><p>Downtown and the Near South/West sides boomed because commercial density, transit infrastructure and capital deployment paved the way for residential demand.</p><p>To genuinely stabilize and grow Black communities in Chicago, the focus must extend beyond housing stock to a comprehensive economic playbook:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-c32274f1-959f-11f1-b174-474306879b2e" start="1"><li><b>Commercial anchor priority:</b> Retail, healthcare and job centers must lead. As seen in the historic revitalization of Pullman, commercial and industrial investment create the payroll base that allows residents to buy and maintain homes.<br></li><li><b>Mixed-use density over isolated housing:</b> Capital should target transit-oriented microdcorridors that combine ground-floor local commerce with residential units above, restoring walkability and essential neighborhood services like groceries and pharmacies.<br></li><li><b>Ownership over tenancy:</b> Reversing wealth loss requires aggressively expanding pathways to homeownership and property acquisition (using land trusts and vacant lot infill programs) rather than overrelying on subsidized rental developments.</li></ol><p>Rebuilding Chicago's Black population base isn't just about building walls; it's about building the financial ecosystem that allows residents to build generational wealth and stay.</p><p><i>Robert Williams, Roseland</i></p><h3>Fears about decline of reading unfounded </h3><p>The current fears of “the end of reading” and “post-literacy" relate to changing social organization and technologies of communications.</p><p>The Atlantic’s Rose Horowitch's recent piece headlined<a class="Link" href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/08/reading-crisis-postliterate-age/687618/" target="_blank" > “The End of Reading Is Here”</a> and New York Times’ David Wallace-Wells’ column headlined <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/16/opinion/reading-test-scores-smartphones.html" target="_blank" >“Is This What a Post-Literate Era Looks Like?”</a> summarize those fears.</p><p>There has never been a single form of literacy and such fears have always persisted.</p><p>The classics were dictated to white slaves, not written by individual authors. "The Odyssey" is a distillation of oral folk tales collected by Homer. Plato and Socrates, among many, feared the impact of writing on comprehension and memory.</p><p>Until the 19th century, most reading remained oral and collective. This included schoolrooms, churches and homes. In factories, one worker read to peers, especially daily newspapers.</p><p>Fears about the decline or “end” of reading followed radio in 1920s and television in 1950s. They accompanied the internet, social media and artificial intelligence eras. Yet, we fail to expect changing forms of literacy.</p><p>Outcries that students and their elders do not — and often cannot — read repeat. Part of “culture wars,” they are intolerant of change. They are supported by misleading exams and studies, and the “reading wars” of different forms of phonics versus phonetics instruction. Screen reading and audio are not counted as forms of reading.</p><p>Young people learn to read in many different ways, including via pictures and sounds. New technologies benefit many of them, including those who are differently abled.</p><p>Students and adults do read. <a class="Link" href="https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/by-topic/industry-news/financial-reporting/article/99417-print-book-sales-rose-slightly-in-2025.html" target="_blank" >Book sales do rise</a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/is-reading-your-favourite-hobby-a-new-era-of-book-clubs-is-reshaping-how-we-read-274406" target="_blank" >book clubs</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USIMLS/bulletins/3f09e4a" target="_blank" >library use have increased</a>.</p><p>Skeptics rarely ask<b>, </b>“what is reading?” across media and different texts. There is no one form of reading. That students need to learn to read different texts differently is seldom considered.</p><p>There is no place for diverse human reading realities in today's “illiteracy myths.” That must change.</p><p><i>Harvey J. Graff, professor emeritus of English and History, Ohio State University, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>Ordinance would help ousted renters</h3><p>I am a tenant who supports Mayor Brandon Johnson’s<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/27/renters-protection-ordinances-mayor-brandon-johnson-aldermanic-opponents-dueling-versions-chicago-city-council" > Protecting Renters Ordinance</a>. The ordinance includes “just cause” provisions — an essential protection for tenants. Currently, tenants live under the reality that their landlord could choose not to renew their lease for any reason, making housing for tenants less secure.</p><p>Under the just cause provisions, a landlord would need to provide one of four reasons for not renewing a lease, along with relocation assistance. Those reasons:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-3bab11a1-95a7-11f1-983e-9d46f145b620" start="1"><li>Owner or a relative is moving into the unit </li><li> Rehab/repair</li><li> Condo conversion</li><li> Removal from the market</li></ol><p>The Just cause provisions are essential to mitigate gentrification, i.e., the large-scale displacement of working class people from their homes by corporate landlords and subsequent rise of housing costs. Many landlords buy buildings at low cost, terminate current tenants’ leases, then raise the rent. For those who are displaced, being uprooted can be economically and emotionally devastating.</p><p>At the City Council's Housing and Real Estate Committee hearing earlier this summer, advocates for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/29/mayor-brandon-johnson-renter-protection-proposal-building-owners-opposition" >smaller mom-and-pop landlords</a> expressed concerns about the cost of the ordinance. But relocation assistance would only be triggered by one of the reasons in the above list. Small landlords, who hold <a class="Link" href="https://www.housingstudies.org/releases/patterns-lost-2-4-unit-buildings-chicago/" target="_blank" >35% of the rental supply, per the DePaul Institute for Housing Studies</a>, will use no-fault lease terminations infrequently and will pay less relocation assistance. In contrast, corporate landlords, who hold the rest of the rental supply, rely on no-fault lease nonrenewals as part of their business model.</p><p>Just cause is not radical. It has been enacted in <a class="Link" href="https://nlihc.org/resource/lawmakers-chicago-introduce-just-cause-eviction-protections-tenants-legislative-session" target="_blank" >11 states and over 25 municipalities</a> in the country. All businesses are regulated for health and safety. Why should landlords be different? </p><p><i>Rachael Wilson,  Bridgeport</i></p><h3>Winning</h3><h3></h3><p>How’s your family farm improving?<br>How’s our new “forever war?”<br>How great is your price for fuel?<br>Next month will it cost more?</p><p>How’s the price of fertilizer?<br>How’s your new high price for feed?<br>How’s doing all the work yourself?<br>Since ICE kidnapped your team</p><p>How great’s your rural hospital?<br>How’s your access to healthcare?<br>How’s your mental health been doing?<br>How’s it feel when no one cares?</p><p>Could AI steal your job next year?<br>How’s that data center next door?<br>The whole neighborhood’s polluted<br>And there's a never-ending roar</p><p>How’s your VA clinic improving?<br>With no nurses or doctors around?<br>Suicide hotline wait times get longer<br>When they shut call centers down</p><p>How great’s high mortgage rates?<br>How great is your spiking rent?<br>How’s your shi—y, little apartment?<br>Forty-five — can’t buy a house yet?</p><p>How great is life in your police state?<br>Masked feds in your neighborhood?<br>How's it being surveilled, searched, seized?<br>Do civil rights violations feel good?</p><p>How’s your tanking dollar value?<br>How great’s your food security?<br>How great are SNAP's reduced benefits?<br>How’s the balance on your EBT?</p><p>And how great’s no more abortions?<br>How great are your 10 grandkids?<br>You feed and house them now?<br>You’re 60 doing a lifetime bid.</p><p>How great’s the kids’ school funding?<br>Illiterate, but know who to hate?<br>How great’s winning what you voted for?<br>Just so you could discriminate.</p><p><i>Nathan Kempthorne, Navy and Air Force veteran, Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Vaccine vacuousness</h3><p>Tuesday's Sun Times had an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/10/trump-signs-executive-order-calling-for-spacing-out-childhood-shots" >Associated Press story</a> about President Donald Trump signing an executive order that recommends separating three childhood vaccines into three shots done at three different office visits. This decision, based on reports, have no scientific advantages. To the contrary, it raises concerns in the legitimate medical circles that it could put children at risk due to delays in decades-long proven vaccines.</p><p>There are other consequences. Parents would have to make three office visits instead of one. This likely will lead to missed time from jobs and the added expenses that result, as well as decreased production. Also, with the cost of healthcare soaring and cuts being made by this administration, insurance companies will now be on the hook for three office visits instead of one. For those who don't have insurance, it'll be a huge financial undertaking. Then there's the fact that tripling the number of visits will make it harder to schedule appointments for physicians who will see their workload tripled. </p><p>These are the consequences that arise from having a president and health secretary who ignore science to push their dangerous personal agendas. Hopefully, for those of us who trust science, the choice of receiving all three vaccines in one visit will still be an option.</p><p><i>John Farrell, DeKalb</i></p><h3>Fauci’s foes set bad precedent</h3><p>Those intent on prosecuting Dr. Anthony Fauci deny the dangers during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic and are still incensed that people had to wear masks, schools were closed and remote learning became a thing. Agreed, it wasn't an easy time, but that's because we were dealing with a global pandemic!</p><p>Many of us remember the severity of the pandemic, especially those of us who lost loved ones. I miss my friend Antoinette every day. She was like a mom to me, but COVID took her. Dr. Fauci worked tirelessly to prevent deaths like hers. Back in 2020, people thanked doctors and nurses for their unwavering devotion. Where is the thanks now? Denial that it was that bad and holding the doctor who helped us through it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/08/06/senate-committee-votes-to-hold-fauci-in-contempt-for-refusing-to-answer-covid-questions" target="_blank" >in contempt?</a></p><p>These unwarranted attacks on Dr. Fauci make me feel as though I am trapped in a horror movie. The next time we face a global outbreak, who will dare to lead us in making the best choices based on scientific research if there's a threat of imprisonment? I fear for Dr. Fauci, but I fear for the rest of us, too.</p><p><i>Diane O'Neill, North Center</i></p><h3>Birthright bias?</h3><p>So do President Donald Trump and Stephen Miller's efforts to <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-trumps-new-attempt-to-limit-birthright-citizenship" target="_blank" >limit birthright citizenship</a> through executive orders apply to white babies, or just babies of color?</p><p><i>Gael Mennecke, Beverly</i></p><h3>Appreciation for two Sun-Times vets</h3><p>Thanks for two Sun-Times treasures: Lee Bey and Neil Steinberg.</p><p>I so appreciated Lee for explaining the status of the two towers at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/08/10/chicago-spire-exterior-construction-two-towers-related-400-n-lake-shore-drive" >400 N. Lake Shore Drive</a>. And when I visited the Steelworkers Park recently, I knew about it because of Lee's writing.</p><p><i>Beth Najberg, Near North Side</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Photojournalism Intern Jeremy Battle. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/big_blocboy_jb/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>The community of Portage, Indiana, was ravaged by severe storms Tuesday. Heavy winds brought down over 100 trees and power lines, landing on homes and vehicles. The community was left without power, internet and cell service for days. Among the worst of the damage was a home on Harrison Avenue that exploded during the storm. The only person home at the time was Leona Rice, 88, who died in the accident. The city is still trying to determine the cause of the explosion. On Wednesday, they began picking up the pieces.</p><h3><b>How did you get this photo?</b></h3><p>Reporter Elijah James and I arrived at the scene among other reporters and city workers clearing the debris. The nearly hour-long drive to Portage had been marred by heavy rain, and by the time we got there it had only dissipated a little. Amid the rain and fallen trees in the yard of nearly every home, most residents stayed inside, peering through windows, to see the press. We went door to door, finding the few who were outside, taking cover under awnings and garage doors. It was important that I presented myself as a person first and a photographer second, as I never wanted to bring a voyeuristic lens to their community’s suffering. I focused on wide angles, trying to document the full breadth of damage caused by the storm.</p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" entries.title: El-Sayed, Mamdani's messages resonate, sending conservatives — and some Dems — into a tailspin
entries.summary: <p>They were articulate, charming and exceptionally gifted. </p><p>But not everyone was immediately enchanted by the dark-haired foreigners in single-breasted suits and skinny ties.</p><p>Many Americans, especially the older adults accustomed to pushing their <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/beatles-suck-yeah-we-said-227748" target="_blank" >staid preferences</a> onto the masses, reacted with blatant hostility, seething over the frenzied adoration that followed the newcomers wherever they went. </p><p>An acclaimed TV host called the foursome <a class="Link" href="https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/sep-keyword/william-f-buckley/" target="_blank" >“the most repulsive group of men I’ve ever seen.” </a></p><p>A few years later, a legendary icon who no longer excited the youth <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehousehistory.org/photos/fotoware?id=8DDA1F4A9CD6481D%2091A1B879AC442BD5" target="_blank" >went to the Oval Office</a> to warn the president that these men "promoted an anti-American spirit."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-620000" name="module-620000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The Beatles are no longer the enemy for the pearl-clutching peanut gallery. </p><p>They've been replaced by young goateed American Muslim men who are challenging and subverting political norms.</p><p>And like the past-his-prime Elvis running to Richard Nixon to rebuke the Liverpudlians and "Communist brainwashing," the usual right-wing suspects and many centrist Democrats are <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/aug/06/abdul-el-sayed-michigan-victory" target="_blank" >ringing the alarm bells</a> over the Brown men while the orange man in the White House sets the country on fire.</p><p>"Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,"<a class="Link" href="https://x.com/RepNancyMace/status/2085825873479893276?s=20" target="_blank" > Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C, posted on X</a> after Abdul El-Sayed <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/abdul-el-sayed-wins-michigans-democratic-senate-primary-notching-midwe-rcna589750" target="_blank" >defeated</a> Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary less than two weeks ago. </p><p>It didn't take long for the president to weigh in.</p><p>"Two VERY DIFFERENT America's, Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117063162955258981" target="_blank" >posted on Truth Social</a> last weekend next to a picture of himself and Melania Trump and another photo of El-Sayed, and his wife, <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/abdul-el-sayed-family-wife-sarah-jukaku-kids-parents-12288396" target="_blank" >Sarah Jukaku</a>, wearing a hijab.</p><p>Who knew Trump could multitask so seamlessly, flexing his xenophobic talents with his ineptitude for proper grammar?</p><p>I don't want to diminish the rampant Islamophobia and death threats that have hounded Reps. <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/12/1/ilhan-omar-plays-death-threat-after-islamophobic-comments" target="_blank" >Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/story/2019/03/17/muslims-rashida-tlaib-congress-1224168" target="_blank" >Rashida Tlaib</a>, D-Mich., and other Muslim politicians. </p><p>I'm also well aware that it is open season for all <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/aug/06/abdul-el-sayed-michigan-victory" target="_blank" >progressive candidate</a>s of any race or religion who champion affordability and denounce corporations, the billionaire class and military aid to Israel.</p><p>But there's no denying the uncs and Karens across the United States have been spiraling ever since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/06/14/new-york-city-mayoral-elections-zohran-mamdani-muslim-indian-gaza-palestinians-cuomo-rummana-column" >Zohran Mamdani</a> was elected New York City mayor last year.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/11/06/nx-s1-5598387/billionaires-who-spent-millions-to-block-him-now-face-working-with-nycs-new-mayor" target="_blank" >$40 million</a> Wall Street CEOs, super PACs and business leaders put up in an effort to keep the democratic socialist from ascending didn't pay off.</p><p>Neither did the <a class="Link" href="https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/07/how-michigan-became-most-expensive-democratic-primary-ever-haley-stevens-abdul-el-sayed-aipac/" target="_blank" >$60 million</a> from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/03/21/aipac-israel-gaza-palestinians-illinois-primary-elections-natalie-moore" >American Israel Public Affairs Committee </a>and other special-interest groups intended to sink El-Sayed. </p><p>To paraphrase Paul McCartney, <a class="Link" href="https://www.thebeatles.com/cant-buy-me-love" target="_blank" >money can’t buy you love</a>. Authenticity does. So does the ability to instill hope for economic equity and global justice.</p><h3></h3><h3>Messages strike a chord</h3><p>Mamdani and El-Sayed's intelligence and eloquence resonate with voters who are barely making ends meet while watching Congress cut checks for bombs used to <a class="Link" href="https://costsofwar.watson.brown.edu/costs/human" target="_blank" >kill mostly Middle Eastern Muslims overseas.</a></p><p>The stereotypes of the dour, sexist and violent Muslim man don't fit, threatening some of the same <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2008/08/06/93329959/poll-white-voters-see-obama-risky-mccain-safe" target="_blank" ><u>Americans who freaked out</u></a> nearly 20 years ago when a dynamic Black man walked into the White House.</p><p>As El-Sayed campaigns against his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, he has been and will continually be <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/09/el-sayed-disavows-pikers-9-11-comments-01030266" target="_blank" >urged to condemn</a> Hasan Piker, the brash, popular Muslim left-wing Twitch streamer who stumped for El-Sayed at previous events. </p><p>The scenario should sound familiar. In 2008, Barack Obama, then in a presidential primary battle with Hillary Clinton, was pressured to <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/story/2008/05/obama-defends-response-to-wright-010068" target="_blank" >cut ties</a> with his pastor, the Rev. Jeremiah Wright, after video recordings of Wright's years-old<a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/wright-defends-sermons-as-debate-over-race-continues" target="_blank" > sermons </a>surfaced.</p><p>Wright berated U.S. foreign policy and systemic racism in the clips.</p><p>"You cannot do terrorism on other people and expect it never to come back on you," Wright <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/wright-defends-sermons-as-debate-over-race-continues" target="_blank" >later said, defending</a> a particular sermon where he said the 9/11 attacks were a consequence of America's past actions halfway around the world. </p><p>Seven years ago, Piker <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6024548-piker-comments-impact-el-sayed/" target="_blank" >made a similar Sept. 11-related comment</a>, which he has since apologized for, along with some of his other incendiary takes.</p><p>“It was a dumb statement,” El-Sayed said during a recent appearance on NBC News' "Meet the Press." </p><p>"And, of course, I think Hasan, himself, would say that was a dumb statement. He disavowed it."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c10000" name="image-c10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b6a08e6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5452x3060+0+288/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4d%2Fe9%2Fe5fbdf4d4207aae3eb4365fab35f%2Fap26217075040330.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/134817f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5452x3060+0+288/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4d%2Fe9%2Fe5fbdf4d4207aae3eb4365fab35f%2Fap26217075040330.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5cc9600/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5452x3060+0+288/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4d%2Fe9%2Fe5fbdf4d4207aae3eb4365fab35f%2Fap26217075040330.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A man in a white suit is speaking into a mic. entries.title: Dear Abby: Wife Doesn't Want To Be Around Husband's Grandchildren
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been with my husband, "Ted," for nearly 15 years, married for 11. He has two children, 38 and 33, and I have one who is 32. When we started dating, none of our children planned to have children of their own. I made it clear from the start that I have no desire to be a grandma. I'm a teacher and work with kids all day, every day, and that is enough for me. He said he felt the same way.</p><p>His children now each have two children, while mine has stuck by her decision not to have any. I still have no desire to fill the grandma role. Ted's kids are starting to make remarks about the fact I am not around much, and Ted recently told me this is causing a divide between us.</p><p>I tried to explain that I haven't changed; he has. We have a blast together and enjoy traveling and hanging out with friends, but our couple time is slowly fading away. I'm tired of being the bad guy because I prefer to spend my personal time with adults.</p><p>Should I figure out how to be a single older lady, agree to live separate lives in the same house, or conform and be miserable, babysitting and spending all my free time doing what I absolutely do not want to do? I want my husband back, not the grandpa. — <i>DON'T CALL ME GRANDMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DON'T CALL ME GRANDMA:</b> You can't expect your husband to turn his back on his grandchildren. If the shoe were on the other foot and your daughter had made you a grandmother, there's a good chance you'd feel exactly as he does now.</p><p>Because you and Ted still love each other, divorce doesn't seem like a good solution. Would the two of you consider separating and returning to more of a dating relationship for a few years until Ted's grandkids no longer need a babysitter? That way, you can continue to have fun with him while avoiding the grandma role.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband's distant cousin, whom we haven't seen in more than 20 years, recently contacted us to say she wants to come for a visit. We have never really cared for her and do not want her to stay with us. Is there a polite way to tell her we are not open for her visit? — <i>KEEPING TO OURSELVES IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR KEEPING:</b> The polite way to tell this distant cousin you do not want her as a houseguest would be to respond that you are unable to host her and suggest some nice hotels in the area. Add that you would be glad to take her out for lunch or dinner in order to catch up while she's in the neighborhood.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> If a woman asks a man to go on a first date, how should the check be paid? — <i>SADIE IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SADIE:</b> The person who offers the invitation is expected to pay for the meal unless there is a prior arrangement to handle it differently. This applies in all relationships, not just romantic ones, but close friends usually have a standing agreement to request separate checks.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: White Sox activate catcher Jake Rogers, demote Edgar Quero for third time this season
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — For the third time this season, Edgar Quero is the odd man out behind the plate.</p><p>On Saturday, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> added Jake Rogers to the 26-man roster and optioned Quero to Triple-A Charlotte. The Sox claimed Rogers off waivers from the Red Sox on Friday and designated left-hander Joe Rock for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster. He's in the lineup and batting ninth. He'll wear No. 28.</p><p>The Sox sent Quero down June 22 when Kyle Teel returned from injuries and Aug. 4 after they traded for Joey Bart. Quero was called back up when Teel sprained his ankle and then when Bart broke his hand.</p><p>Quero is hitting .208/.279/.262 with three home runs in 65 games this season. He has been hot lately, hitting .370 with a .933 OPS in his last eight games. But the Sox <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/11/catcher-drew-romo-chicago-white-sox-anthony-kay-walker-mckinven" target="_blank" >much prefer Drew Romo’s defense</a> behind the plate, despite his lower production at the plate. Romo is hitting .132/.214/.285. </p><p>The Red Sox designated Rogers for assignment Tuesday. The 31-year-old, who also has played for the Tigers and Orioles this season, is hitting .183/.290/.327 with three homers in 42 games.</p><p>"Really good defensive catcher," manager Will Venable said. "I think that you look at our catching unit and to be able to add depth is really important for us. [He's] a guy who has had a lot of success in this league, really understands what it means to help a pitcher navigate a game, still productive against left-handed pitching."<br></p>
